name: Respond to roadside breakdowns
summary: When a tractor or trailer breaks down on the highway, the driver secures the scene and calls in, and the maintenance breakdown desk decides within minutes whether the driver can fix it, a company road technician or a contracted mobile repair or tire service should go, or the unit must be towed. Most calls are tires, brakes, lights, hoses and engine cooling faults fixed in about an hour once help arrives; the time is lost waiting for help to reach the unit, especially at night, in winter and on remote highways. A tow also means finding replacement power to recover the load and telling the customer it will be late.

baseline.org_archetype: A Canadian LTL and truckload carrier of about 3,000 employees with twelve company maintenance shops at its hubs and larger terminals, about 1,190 company power units and 4,120 trailers.
baseline.notes: Calls come from company truckload and linehaul tractors and from owner-operators who use the carrier's breakdown desk. City trucks that fail near their terminal are usually handled by the terminal shop and are a small share.

trigger: A driver phones in a breakdown on the road.
end_state: The unit is running again, or towed to a shop with a repair work order open, and any vendor or tow invoice is matched and passed to payables.

volume.seasonality: Highest from December to March (cold starts, gelled fuel, air system freezes, tire damage) and in summer heat for cooling faults.

evidence.note: TMC/FleetNet benchmarks give about 64,800 miles between roadside repairs for LTL fleets and 14,300 to 34,600 for truckload fleets (2019-2020). At an assumed 2.1 million linehaul miles and 3.6 million company truckload miles a month this gives about 30 LTL and 100 to 250 truckload calls; owner-operator calls handled by the desk and trailer and tire calls bring the total to the organisation file's 240 to 380. Mileages are the author's estimate.

surge.cause: Winter storm or highway closure (snowstorms, freezing rain, mountain pass closures)

evidence.note: Taken from the organisation file's surge estimate for this process.

Organisation file role (headcount 300); title, cost and shift from the organisation file, which loads wages by 1.30 for hourly staff and 1.35 for salaried staff. Stands for the driver of the broken-down unit; about 60% of calls come from truckload drivers and 40% from LTL linehaul drivers, who do the same steps.

Organisation file role (headcount 8); title, cost and shift from the organisation file, which loads wages by 1.30 for hourly staff and 1.35 for salaried staff. Takes breakdown calls outside office hours; in the day the driver manager or linehaul dispatcher takes the call the same way.

The organisation file has no role for this work. Carriers of this size run a 24-hour maintenance breakdown desk (often called road call or road service coordinators) that troubleshoots with the driver, chooses the repair and sends help. About five people cover the desk around the clock; about 2.6 FTE of their time is spent on calls. Cost set like a linehaul dispatcher.

Organisation file role (headcount 14); title, cost and shift from the organisation file, which loads wages by 1.30 for hourly staff and 1.35 for salaried staff. On-call technicians with a service truck attend about 30% of calls near company terminals.

Organisation file role (headcount 14); title, cost and shift from the organisation file, which loads wages by 1.30 for hourly staff and 1.35 for salaried staff. Approves costly tows and repairs and receives towed units.

Organisation file role (headcount 36); title, cost and shift from the organisation file, which loads wages by 1.30 for hourly staff and 1.35 for salaried staff. Arranges replacement power or a recovery driver for the load and tells the customer of the delay.

Organisation file role (headcount 8); title, cost and shift from the organisation file, which loads wages by 1.30 for hourly staff and 1.35 for salaried staff. Matches vendor invoices to road call purchase orders the next working days.

systems.name: Fleet maintenance management system (work orders, PM schedules, parts)
Transportation management system (LTL and truckload operations, billing, rating)
Electronic logging devices and telematics platform
Email, phone system and contact centre software

steps.name: Pull over and secure the scene
steps.description: When a warning light, loss of power, air leak or tire failure occurs, the driver pulls onto the shoulder or the nearest safe place, switches on the hazard lights, sets out warning triangles behind the unit and checks the problem.

control.basis: Provincial highway traffic rules requiring warning devices around a disabled commercial vehicle

evidence.note: Warning devices must be placed when a commercial vehicle is stopped on a highway under provincial rules; minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Call in the breakdown
steps.description: The driver phones the dispatch or breakdown line and gives the unit number, location (highway, nearest exit or kilometre marker), the symptoms and the dashboard codes, the load and its delivery time, and whether the unit is in a safe place.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Take the call and log it
steps.description: The dispatcher opens the trip in the TMS, notes the breakdown and location against the load, checks the delivery appointment and the driver's remaining hours, and transfers the call to the maintenance breakdown desk.

error.defect_description: Location recorded imprecisely, which delays the vendor or tow.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Troubleshoot and choose the response
steps.description: The road call coordinator talks the driver through checks, reads live fault codes and location from the telematics platform, looks up the unit's warranty and repair history, and decides whether the driver can fix it, a company road technician should go, a third-party mobile repair or tire service should be called, or the unit must be towed.

error.defect_description: Wrong response chosen (vendor sent for a fault that needs a tow), adding hours.

next.condition: third-party mobile repair or tire service
storm or road closure: help cannot reach the unit yet

evidence.note: Tires, brakes, lighting, power plant and cooling make up most roadside repairs, and a typical roadside call often includes a tow (TMC/FleetNet); response shares are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Coach the driver through a fix
steps.description: The coordinator talks the driver through a simple fix (resetting a fault, reconnecting an air or electrical line, replacing a fuse or bulb, regenerating the particulate filter) and confirms the warning has cleared.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Call out the road service technician
steps.description: The coordinator phones the on-call road service technician, gives the location, symptoms and likely parts, and agrees an arrival time with the driver.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Drive to the breakdown
steps.description: The road service technician loads likely parts on the service truck and drives to the unit, often at night and in winter conditions on highways near the terminal.

evidence.note: Fourteen road service technicians and trucks in the organisation file; travel and wait for a free technician are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Repair at the roadside
steps.description: Wearing high-visibility gear and using the truck's beacons for traffic protection, the technician diagnoses and repairs the fault on the shoulder: replaces a hose, belt, air line, lamp or tire, or makes a temporary repair that lets the unit reach a shop.

control.basis: Roadside work-zone protection under provincial occupational health and safety and highway traffic rules

next.condition: cannot be fixed on the road

evidence.note: Average roadside repair time 1.1 hours in the TMC/FleetNet benchmark (Q4 2019); the range and share needing a tow are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Engage a third-party vendor
steps.description: The coordinator calls mobile repair or tire service vendors near the location from the approved vendor list, compares arrival times and rates, gives the vendor a purchase order number and passes the arrival time to the driver.

next.condition: vendor slow to confirm or late: chase

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Chase the vendor and update the driver
steps.description: The coordinator phones the vendor for an updated arrival time, tries another vendor if the first cannot come, and keeps the driver and the dispatcher informed so the delivery appointment can be moved.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Vendor travels and repairs
steps.description: The vendor drives to the unit and repairs it on the shoulder, most often a tire, brake, light or hose; the vendor's time is billed to the carrier.

next.condition: cannot be fixed on the road

evidence.note: Roadside repair takes about an hour once on scene (TMC/FleetNet); travel and arrival times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Arrange a tow
steps.description: The coordinator chooses a heavy-tow operator that covers the area, agrees the rate and the destination (the nearest company shop or the dealer for warranty work), and tells the driver what to expect.

next.condition: tow or repair above the coordinator's limit

evidence.note: Average tow cost about US$1,485 (TMC/FleetNet); minutes and share above the spending limit are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Approve the tow or repair cost
steps.description: The on-call shop foreman reviews the tow quote or repair estimate against the unit's value and warranty and approves it or asks the coordinator to find a cheaper option.

control.basis: Company spending authority limits for road calls and tows

evidence.note: Spending limits for road calls are common practice; author's estimate.

steps.name: Tow operator arrives and tows
steps.description: The tow operator travels to the unit, often far from town and in winter weather, hooks up the tractor or the combination and tows it to the shop or dealer.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; night and winter calls on remote highways take longest, per the organisation file's process description.

steps.name: Arrange replacement power and recover the load
steps.description: While the unit is towed, the driver manager finds a spare tractor or another driver to recover the trailer and finish the delivery, re-plans the driver's next load, and has customer service tell the consignee the new arrival time.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Receive the towed unit and open a repair order
steps.description: The shop foreman checks the towed unit in, records its condition and opens a repair work order for the defect repair queue, attaching the coordinator's notes and fault codes.

next.condition: unit handed to the shop; tow invoice is matched on the repair work order

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Record the roadside repair
steps.description: The coordinator records what was done, the parts, the vendor or technician time and the purchase order in the fleet maintenance system, and opens a follow-up work order when the fix was temporary.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Check the unit and resume the trip
steps.description: The driver walks around the unit, checks that the warning has cleared and nothing is leaking, records the delay on the logbook or ELD, and continues the trip or drives to the nearest shop for a permanent repair.

next.condition: no invoice (driver fix or company technician)

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Match the road call invoice
steps.description: When the vendor or tow operator's invoice arrives, the maintenance planner matches it to the purchase order and road call record, checks hours, mileage charges and parts against the quote, codes it to the unit and passes it to accounts payable.

evidence.note: Invoices arrive days after the call; author's estimate.

steps.name: Wait out the storm or road closure
steps.description: When a storm or highway closure stops tow trucks and technicians from reaching the unit, the coordinator keeps in touch with the driver, checks that the driver is safe and warm, and holds the response until the road reopens.

next.condition: road reopened, choose the response again

evidence.note: Storms close Highway 401, the Trans-Canada through the Rockies and the Coquihalla several times each winter (organisation file surge); duration is the author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Tow after a failed roadside repair
exceptions.description: The technician or vendor cannot fix the unit on the shoulder and it is towed after all, adding hours.

exceptions.name: Storm or road closure
exceptions.description: Help cannot reach the unit until the highway reopens; the driver waits in the cab.

exceptions.name: Vendor late or unavailable
exceptions.description: The first vendor cannot come or is late and the coordinator chases or finds another.

exceptions.name: Cost above the coordinator's limit
exceptions.description: A long tow or large repair needs the on-call foreman's approval.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from call to call closed (invoice matched where there is one)
benchmarks.population: Breakdown calls at a Canadian LTL and truckload carrier, 2019-2022

evidence.note: Author's estimate: most calls end when the unit is running again or reaches a shop, usually four to ten hours after the call; vendor-repaired calls close when the invoice is matched days later.

benchmarks.unit: hours of repair time per roadside event

evidence.note: Up from 0.9 hours six months earlier.

benchmarks.population: LTL fleets in the TMC/FleetNet benchmark, Q4 2019

evidence.note: Truckload dry van fleets averaged 14,333 miles in the same report.

benchmarks.unit: times the cost of the same repair in the fleet's own shop
benchmarks.population: Truckload fleets in the TMC/FleetNet program, 2018

pain_points.description: Waiting for a vendor or tow to reach the unit, at night, in winter and on remote highways, is most of the downtime.

evidence.note: Named in the organisation file's process description; author's estimate.

pain_points.description: Roadside repairs cost about four times as much as the same repair in the company's shop.

evidence.note: TMC/FleetNet program, 2018.

pain_points.description: Vague locations and symptoms from the driver send the wrong help.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

pain_points.description: Vendor invoices arrive late and with extra hours or mileage that must be checked against the call record.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

assumptions: The organisation file names a 'shop dispatcher' in the process description but has no such role; this workflow adds a breakdown and road call coordinator (not in the organisation file) on a 24-hour desk.
Driver steps use the long-haul truckload driver; LTL linehaul drivers and owner-operators do the same steps.
Vendor and tow operator time is entered as waiting time on external steps (their labour is billed, not paid as wages), so it counts in elapsed time but not in the carrier's hands-on time.

About a third of calls generate a vendor invoice matched in s17; driver fixes and company technician calls do not, and tow invoices are matched on the shop repair work order after the unit is towed in.

The workflow adds fin-accounts-payable (vendor invoices) and tl-load-planning (replacement equipment) as receivers; the organisation file lists only defect repair work orders and tow requests. Tow operators' invoices already reach payables directly in the organisation file.
Simulated cycle time includes the days until a vendor invoice is matched for about a third of calls; the unit itself is usually moving again within hours.

sources.title: TMC20: Unscheduled truck maintenance costs rising
sources.supports: TMC and FleetNet America benchmark, Q4 2019: average roadside repair cost US$450 (US$358 a year earlier); average tow cost US$1,485; roadside repair time rose from 0.9 to 1.1 hours; miles between roadside repairs 14,333 for truckload dry van fleets, 64,768 for LTL fleets and 44,303 for tank fleets; tires, brakes, lighting, power plant and cooling systems account for 65% of repairs.

sources.title: Study: Roadside truck breakdowns occur every 10,000 miles
sources.supports: TMC and FleetNet America BenchMarkit program (truckload fleets, 2018): about 10,000 miles between breakdown events; average roadside repair event cost US$334 in Q4 2018 excluding tires; roadside repairs cost about four times as much as the same repair in the fleet's own shop; most frequent systems are cooling, wheels and hubs, brakes, lighting and tires.

sources.title: 4 Ways to Improve Fleet Uptime
sources.supports: TMC/FleetNet benchmarking for Q3 2020: 34,629 miles between unscheduled roadside repairs for the average fleet; top five systems 72% of roadside repairs; LTL average cost per mechanical roadside repair US$642; top LTL fleets have 34% fewer breakdowns than the average LTL fleet.
